name: prop-rig-getting-started
description: "Use on first run with a new owner: onboard them one question at a time, list what they provide, and run the first Prop & Rig Director grade with the lens engine."
---

> **Audit contract v1 (overrides everything below).** Created by @meta_alchemist (https://x.com/meta_alchemist).
> - Score only with the rubric embedded in `engine/lens.mjs` (`LENS.rubric`, gbf-03-procedural-rig-crafter v1.3.0). `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` computes the grade; this skill only gathers evidence for it and never adds points of its own.
> - Missing evidence is UNMEASURED (0 points, not a defect). A test that did not run is NOT_RUN, never PASS. Never invent a measurement; label every worked example synthetic.
> - Game facts and budgets come from your game profile (`pack.profile`). Treat sample numbers as illustrative. Set the frame-time budget separately for each target device in your game profile.
> - An automated gate needs a negative fixture that fails. Receipts carry measured values, never an unconditional PASS.
> Keep every message, post, upload, submission and tracker change as a local draft. Only the human reviews and sends, publishes, uploads or files it. Work only on a working branch. Push only when the human asks and only to that branch. Never push to main. The human merges and deploys. Any feature switch you add is off by default.

# Prop & Rig Director: Getting Started

Build and optimize props and rigs for your runtime. Compare their appearance, animation and collision shapes with your art and performance targets.

A prop is any modelled object in the game world: furniture, vehicles, plants, tools, creatures, buildings, doors, crates or held items. A rig is the set of joints that lets a prop or character animate. This template is for 3D assets (including 3D models in a 2D-looking game). For flat 2D sprites, use the 2D Sprite Atlas & Hitbox Packer template (17) instead.

If `engine/lens.mjs`, `engine/lens-kit.mjs` or `fixtures/good-pack.json` are not on disk yet, write them byte for byte from the `prop-rig-lens-engine` skill first (Node 18+, no dependencies).

## 1. Onboard one question at a time

Ask one question at a time, wait for the answer, then ask the next. Never stack questions in one message. Give no setup steps until question 2 is answered.

1. Which game are we reviewing, and which kinds of props does it need (for example furniture, vehicles, plants, tools, creatures, buildings or held items)? After the answer, ask for the build to review (a build ID, commit or version), then ask where the evidence will come from (a CI job, an editor script or manual captures).
2. Which engine and asset pipeline do you use today? For example Unity, Unreal, Godot, Blender exporting FBX or glTF, or Three.js with glTF. Use only the matching pipeline from now on. If there is no pipeline yet, ask the owner to pick one; do not install tools or change project settings on your own.
3. Do any props attach to an animated character or move through extreme poses (a held tool, a backpack, a saddle, a swinging door)? If none do, we use the `static-props` profile: `silhouette:2` (held prop at extreme poses) and `animation-and-weapon-clearance:1` (pose clipping) read N/A, not U and not defects, and their partner lines take each pillar's 20 points.
4. Do props or characters stand on slopes or uneven ground? If all walkable ground is flat, the profile can list only `0` in `requiredSlopesDeg`.
5. How closely must a collision shape match the visible model, and how deep may one part pass into another before it counts as clipping? (These set `minColliderIoU` and `maxPenetrationCm`.)
6. Which art reference is current (a file name or version), so palette and scale checks compare against the right one?
7. Which values go in the rest of your game profile (`pack.profile`)? Start from the synthetic profile in `fixtures/good-pack.json` and go through the other keys in the table below one at a time. Confirm or replace each value; never keep a sample number without the owner saying so.
8. Who reviews the local finding drafts?

| Profile key | What it means |
|---|---|
| `minSilhouetteContrast` | Lowest contrast allowed between a prop's outline and the background behind it at the gameplay camera. |
| `minSilhouettePx` | Smallest on-screen height, in pixels, at which a prop must still be recognisable. |
| `viewports` | The screens you check, for example `desktop` and `phone`. |
| `requiredExtremes` | The extreme poses where a held prop must stay recognisable, for example reach up, crouch or turn. |
| `maxPenetrationCm`, `minimumPoses` | Deepest allowed overlap between an attached part and the body, and how many poses must be checked. |
| `maxFootGapCm`, `requiredSlopesDeg` | Largest allowed gap between a foot or base and the ground, and which slope angles to test. |
| `minColliderIoU` | Minimum overlap between the collision shape and the visible shape. IoU (intersection over union) runs from 0 to 1; 1 is a perfect match. |
| `floorProbeBudgetMs` | Time allowed per frame for the ground check (the ray or shape cast that finds the floor under a character or prop). |
| `frameP95BudgetMs`, `maxDrawCalls` | Frame time that 95 percent of frames must beat, and the draw-call limit, on the target device. |
| `maxLodSwapsPerSecond` | How often a model may switch between levels of detail (LOD, simpler versions shown far away). |
| `maxPaletteDeltaE` | Largest colour difference allowed against the art reference. DeltaE is a standard colour distance; about 2 is barely visible. |

Read the profile pick back to the owner and, once they approve, set it before scoring: `"rubricProfile": ["static-props"]` in `pack.profile`. With every other line at level 3 or more the verdict can then be PASS. Name the profile next to the grade.

Distances are in centimetres of world space. Convert from your engine's units (by convention 1 Unity or Godot unit is 1 metre and 1 Unreal unit is 1 centimetre; glTF uses metres).

Before grading a real pack, check that its build and profile match what the owner chose. Record a capture or run that could not happen as NOT_RUN. Each line needs a sample population (the list of measured cases it reads); `node engine/lens.mjs --meta` lists them.

## 2. What you provide

- An evidence pack (JSON) with `status: "VALID"`, a `liveSha` (the build that was running when you captured), a `gitSha` (the source commit) and a `packId` (all three are required), and an `artifacts` list. Every metric group names the artifact id it came from.
- Metric groups this engine reads: `silhouette` (capture), `attachedPropSilhouette` (capture; the engine's name for any held or attached prop), `clearance` (capture), `grounding` (capture), `colliders` (capture), `probe` (trace), `scene` (trace), `lod` (capture), `artRef` (capture), `variation` (static), `animation` (capture).
- Profile thresholds in `pack.profile`. A missing threshold makes its line U, never a default.
- Anything you cannot capture yet stays out of the pack. It grades U (UNMEASURED), which is honest and costs no false defect. With `static-props` approved, leave `attachedPropSilhouette`, `clearance` and `receipts.poseSweep` out; those lines read N/A. Any other line your game does not need has no profile: leave it out and tell the owner it stays U.

## 3. Run the first grade

```
node engine/lens.mjs fixtures/good-pack.json   # worked example, synthetic, not a measurement
node engine/lens.mjs your-pack.json            # your build
node engine/lens.mjs --meta                    # rubric lines, weights and what each reads
node engine/lens.mjs --fixtures fixtures/good-pack.json  # negative and missing-input self-test
```

Read the record: `verdict` (PASS, CONDITIONAL, BLOCKED or INVALID), `grade` and `coverage`, then each line's `level` and `findings`, then `checks` (growth checks reported beside the grade) and `tickets` (deduplicated candidates).

## 4. Report in plain English

- Lead with the verdict, grade and coverage in one sentence. Say how much of the rubric was measured.
- List U lines as "not measured yet" with the capture that would measure them. Never call them defects.
- One local ticket draft per measured finding, with the pack id and artifact ids. Label any synthetic pack as synthetic.
- Rubric lines: silhouette:1, silhouette:2, animation-and-weapon-clearance:1, animation-and-weapon-clearance:2, collider-agreement:1, collider-agreement:2, scene-budget:1, scene-budget:2, visual-consistency:1, visual-consistency:2. The words "weapon" and "equipped" in some line names cover any held or attached prop.

## 5. Skills in this template

- `procedural-prop-builder`: Build a prop or rig from art references in your engine, with reproducible variation and measurable clearance.
- `asset-lod-and-compression-pipeline`: Make simpler and smaller versions of a 3D asset for your target devices and check that its look, animation and collision still match the original.
- `turntable-collider-proof`: Use after building a prop or rig: prove its collision shape matches the visible model from every angle and that clearance and grounding hold in real poses.
- `entry-scene-optional-interactions`: If your game has a title, menu or hub scene with decorative objects, design optional reactions for them and check that players can still find and use the main action.
- `prop-rig-lens-engine`: the engine source and how to run it.

## Blockers to tell the owner about

- Silhouette and palette numbers need captures from your gameplay camera; the worked example is synthetic.

With only a design reference and no build, draft the capture plan locally and mark the runtime checks NOT_RUN.

Before capture, agree on the test cases in `profile.cases`: for example each collider view, each clip and pose, and each slope, with its case id and expected values. After capture, `receipts` holds one measured row per case with the case id, the `liveSha` of the build that ran, the artifact id and the measured values. Run `node engine/lens.mjs --meta` for the required row fields and comparisons. A skipped or stale case leaves its line U. The bundled rows and budgets are synthetic.

## Team inputs and outputs

This template works on its own. When other templates from the kit run in the same game project, they exchange files under `.grokbot-team/artifacts/<artifact>/` (read the newest file) and share an append-only memory under `.grokbot-team/memory/`. Team spec 1.0.0.

Before acting, look for these inputs:

| Input | From | Where to look | If it is missing |
|---|---|---|---|
| `game-profile` (required, ^1.0.0) | the owner | `pack.profile` in the evidence pack, or `.grokbot-team/artifacts/game-profile/` | Ask the getting-started questions and write it with the owner. A missing threshold leaves its line unmeasured, never a default. |
| `evidence-pack` (required, ^1.0.0) | the owner | the pack path the owner gives, or `.grokbot-team/artifacts/evidence-pack/` | Stop and ask the owner for a pack. Without one there is no grade; record NOT_RUN. |
| `layout-brief` (optional, ^1.0.0) | 11 Environment | `.grokbot-team/artifacts/layout-brief/` | Continue: take the asset list from the owner and write "ASSUMPTION: no layout-brief available; asset list from the owner" in the report. |

After acting, save these outputs as local files for the human to review:

| Output | Format | Where | Read by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `asset-budget-report` 1.0.0 | JSON | `.grokbot-team/artifacts/asset-budget-report/` | 11 Environment |
| `grade-record` 1.0.0 | JSON (the engine's grade record) | `.grokbot-team/artifacts/grade-record/` | 12 Producer |
| `ticket-draft` 1.0.0 | JSON or Markdown local draft | `.grokbot-team/artifacts/ticket-draft/` | 12 Producer, 18 Bug Desk |

Each output file is JSON with `artifact`, `version`, `producer` (this template's id and version), `createdAt` (UTC), `synthetic` and `items`, as the kit's `spec/artifacts/<artifact>.schema.json` describes. Name files `<UTC date>-<short label>.json` so the newest sorts last.

Shared memory:

- Before acting, read `decisions`, `releases` from `.grokbot-team/memory/<topic>.jsonl`. Skip records that have expired or that a later record supersedes.
- Write only `decisions`. Append one line per record with `engine/team-memory.mjs` (or the same JSON by hand): id, UTC time, writer (`gbf-03-procedural-rig-crafter` and `2.0.0`), topic, kind, summary, data, source, confidence (measured, reported or assumed), expires_at and supersedes. Never edit or delete a line; supersede it.
- Never put secrets, names, handles, wallets, emails or raw user ids in memory. Refer to a person or account only by `node engine/team-memory.mjs hash <id>`, which needs the salt in `GROKBOT_TEAM_SALT`. Run `node engine/team-memory.mjs lint` before you finish.
- Keep `.grokbot-team/` out of a public game repository (add it to `.gitignore`); in a private one, commit it so the append-only rule can be checked against history.

# Build a procedural prop or rig

Use this when you assemble a prop from parts, by script or by hand, and want variation that is repeatable and measurable. It feeds `silhouette:1`, `visual-consistency:1`, `visual-consistency:2` and, for animated props, `animation-and-weapon-clearance:1`.

## 0. Ask first

Ask which engine and asset pipeline the project uses before giving any setup step, then use only that row. If the answer is "none yet", ask the owner to choose; do not install tools on your own.

| Pipeline | Parent node for the prop | Seeded variation lives in |
|---|---|---|
| Unity | a prefab with child GameObjects | an editor script or a component that reads a stored seed |
| Unreal | a Blueprint actor with mesh components, or a Static Mesh with sockets | a construction script with a stored seed |
| Godot | a scene with a Node3D root | an editor (tool mode) script or an import script with a stored seed |
| Blender export | an Empty parent with child objects, exported as FBX or glTF | a Python script or Geometry Nodes with a fixed seed |
| Three.js | a `THREE.Group` | the build function that creates the group |

## 1. Build

1. Break the art reference into the shapes the player sees from the gameplay camera. Model those first; small detail comes last.
2. Put all parts under one named parent node. Give every moving joint (a wheel, a lid, a door hinge, a creature's jaw) a stable local pivot.
3. Match the project's world units, up axis, pivot placement and material setup. Check them against one existing asset that already looks right in game.
4. Reuse shared meshes and materials for repeated parts, so ten chairs cost little more than one.
5. Drive decorative variation (wear, colour shift, leaf count) from a seeded random stream. Keep that stream separate from placement and gameplay randomness, so the same seed always gives the same prop.
6. Build collision proxies (simple boxes, capsules or convex hulls) from the gameplay design, not from the fine visual mesh, and show them over the rendered prop.

Short examples (synthetic, for illustration only):

- Farming sim: a fence segment with seeded plank wear. Collision is one thin box; grounding matters on hills.
- Racing game: a car with four wheel pivots and a seeded decal set. Clearance means the wheels never sink into the body when the suspension compresses.
- Narrative adventure: a bookshelf with seeded book colours. No animation; if no prop in the game is held, attached or animated, the owner can approve the `static-props` profile and the pose lines read N/A.
- 3D arena game: a held tool or shield on a character's hand socket. Check it at the extreme poses in the profile.
- Mobile puzzle game with 3D pieces: one rounded block repeated in many colours. Silhouette and draw calls matter most.
- Creature: a jaw and tail rig. Check that the teeth stay outside the head across the bite clip.

## 2. Capture

- The rest pose, the pose with the greatest reach, and the prop at its smallest intended on-screen size.
- For seeded props, two separate export runs with the same seed, and the digest (hash) of each output mesh (`variation.sameSeedHashes`, `receipts.seedRuns`).
- Clearance, draw calls and frame time compared with the game profile.

## 3. Negative fixture

Offset one collision proxy on purpose in a test copy and confirm the overlay shows the mismatch and the check fails. A check that never fails proves nothing.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` (see `prop-rig-lens-engine`). If the asset or tool is not available, record NOT_RUN and keep its numbers out of the pack.

# Optimize a 3D asset

Make lighter versions of an asset (fewer triangles, smaller files, levels of detail) and prove they still look, animate and collide like the original. It feeds `scene-budget:1`, `scene-budget:2` and `silhouette:1`, and re-checks `collider-agreement:1` after the change.

## 0. Ask first

Ask which engine and export pipeline the project uses before giving any command, then use only that row. If a tool in the row is not installed, record NOT_RUN and ask the owner; do not install it on your own.

| Pipeline | Simplify and make LODs (levels of detail) | Compress for delivery | Measure in game |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unity | LOD Group component with simplified meshes | Mesh Compression in the model import settings | Profiler and Frame Debugger |
| Unreal | LOD settings in the Static Mesh editor, or Nanite where your target supports it | the engine's cooked packaging | Unreal Insights, `stat unit` |
| Godot | LOD generation in the glTF or scene import settings | the import settings for meshes and textures | Profiler and Monitors |
| Blender export | Decimate modifier on a copy, exported as extra LOD meshes | done in the target engine | measured in the target engine |
| Three.js with glTF | `gltf-transform simplify` | `gltf-transform draco` or `gltf-transform meshopt`, only if the matching decoder ships with your build | browser performance trace and `renderer.info` |

## 1. Record the starting point

Keep an untouched copy of the original. Record its triangle count, material count, texture bytes, download size, load or decode time and the largest size it appears on screen. Normalise scale and axes to the project's import settings.

## 2. Simplify one step at a time

Make one LOD at a time. Preserve outline edges, skin weights, joint names, animation tracks, sockets and collision markers. Measure file size and decode cost separately: a smaller file that takes longer to decode can be slower overall.

Example from the Three.js row (synthetic, for illustration only):

```sh
gltf-transform simplify original.glb candidate.glb --ratio 0.5
gltf-transform draco candidate.glb candidate-draco.glb
```

Load the candidate with the decoder your game actually ships, not a desktop viewer.

## 3. Compare

Overlay the original and the candidate at matched camera positions. Test shadows, ground contact, extreme joint motion and LOD switches at the distances players really see. Short examples:

- Racing game: a trackside grandstand seen at 200 km/h needs aggressive LODs; check for popping on the straight.
- Farming sim: hundreds of crop plants share one mesh; draw calls and instancing matter more than triangles.
- Mobile puzzle game: one prop on screen at a time; texture bytes and load time matter most.
- Open-world 3D game: buildings switch LOD often; record `lod.swapsPerSecondMax` along a real route.

## 4. Negative fixture and record

Build a test candidate with a missing joint or a moved collider and confirm the comparison fails. Record the chosen export settings, the source format, exporter and decoder versions, and the peak frame time on target hardware. If an asset or tool is unavailable, record NOT_RUN and keep its measurements out of the pack.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` (see `prop-rig-lens-engine`).

# Turntable collider proof

Prove that what the player sees is what the physics touches, before the asset ships. A turntable is a capture where the asset spins in front of a fixed camera so every side is recorded. It feeds `collider-agreement:1`, `animation-and-weapon-clearance:1`, `animation-and-weapon-clearance:2` and `visual-consistency:2`.

## 0. Ask first

Ask which engine the project uses and how it can show collision shapes, then use only that route:

- Unity: the Physics Debugger window, or Gizmos drawn in the Scene view.
- Unreal: the `show collision` view option or console command.
- Godot: Debug, then Visible Collision Shapes.
- Three.js or another web engine: a wireframe helper drawn over the mesh.
- Blender only: render the collision meshes on their own layer; the in-game check stays NOT_RUN until the asset is in the engine.

## Method

1. Render the asset on a turntable with enough yaw (turn) and pitch (tilt) samples to cover its outline, at the gameplay camera distance, with the visible mesh and the collision shape drawn as two aligned masks.
2. For each view, compute IoU (intersection over union: the overlapping area divided by the combined area of the two masks). Store one value per view in `colliders.iou` and one row per approved view in `receipts.colliderViews` with the asset id, view, tool version and the two pixel areas. Report the lowest value with its view and capture id.
3. Pose sweep, only for animated or attached props: play every approved clip to its extremes and measure the deepest overlap into the body, walls, floor or other actors (`clearance.penetrationCm`, `clearance.posesChecked`, `receipts.poseSweep`). Static props (furniture, buildings, rocks) need no sweep. When no prop in the game is held, attached or animated, the owner can approve the `static-props` profile: leave this out and the line reads N/A, not U.
4. Grounding: place the asset on flat ground and on each slope in the profile, and record the largest foot or base gap (`grounding.footGapCm`, `grounding.slopeDegTested`, `receipts.slopeContacts`).
5. Seeded variation: export the same seed in two separate runs and compare their mesh digests (`variation.sameSeedHashes`, `receipts.seedRuns`).

Short examples (synthetic, for illustration only):

- Platformer in 3D: a moving platform whose collision box is taller than its mesh makes players stand on air.
- Racing game: a barrier whose collider sticks out past its mesh stops cars before they touch it.
- Life sim: a sofa whose collider is too small lets characters walk through its arms.
- Shooter or arena game: a crate whose collider is bigger than its mesh blocks shots that look clear.
- Point-and-click 3D adventure: a clickable object whose collider is offset makes clicks miss.

## Negative fixture

In a test copy, inflate the collision shape by a clear margin (for example 30 percent) and confirm the IoU check fails. A gate that never fails proves nothing.

## Pitfalls

- A collider that only matches from the default camera angle hides unfair hits, missed clicks and invisible walls from other angles.
- Thresholds (`minColliderIoU`, `maxPenetrationCm`, `maxFootGapCm`) live in your game profile, not here.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` (see `prop-rig-lens-engine`). If an asset is missing or its format is not supported, return NOT_RUN and name the conversion or export the owner needs to provide.

# Make an interactive entry scene

Use this only if your game has an entry scene: a title screen, main menu, lobby or hub where decorative objects sit around the main controls. If the entry is a plain menu with no scene behind it, skip this skill.

The goal is small optional reactions (a sign tilts when tapped, a cat looks at the cursor) that add charm without slowing the player down. The main action always wins.

## 0. Ask first

Ask, one at a time: what is the player's first task on this screen (for example continue a save, start a level, join a session or pick a puzzle)? Is the scene 2D or 3D, and which engine draws it? Which inputs does the game support (mouse, touch, controller, keyboard)? Then plan only for those answers.

Short examples (synthetic, for illustration only):

- 2D platformer title screen: a parallax forest; a bird hops when the cursor passes. Main action: Start.
- Mobile puzzle game: tiles on the start screen jiggle when tapped. Main action: Play, which must stay the largest tap target.
- Farming or life sim: a farmhouse porch; the mailbox wobbles on focus. Main action: Continue.
- Racing game: a garage; headlights flash when the car is focused. Main action: Race.
- Turn-based strategy game: a map table; flags sway on hover. Main action: Resume campaign.
- 3D menu scene: a shelf of collectibles; one spins when clicked. Main action: Play.

## 1. Design

Place optional interactions away from the main controls and keep focus order stable for every supported input (a controller or keyboard must reach the main action in the same number of steps as before). Choose one reaction that fits the art direction. Limit how many effects can run at once, release temporary audio and animation objects when they finish, and respect reduced-motion and mute settings.

Put the reactions behind a feature switch that is off by default. Before any decorative motion starts, check both the owner's opt-in and the current accessibility setting:

```js
function entranceMotion(ownerOptIn, enabled, reducedMotion) {
  return ownerOptIn === true && enabled === true && reducedMotion === false;
}
```

## 2. Measure

Compare, with and without the reactions: time to reach the main action, accidental activations of decorations, and worst-case frame time. Repeat on the smallest supported display. Test the switch when it is missing, set to an invalid value and set to off; each case must behave exactly like the baseline. Then test the switch on with reduced motion enabled and keep the paired captures.

Negative fixture: in a test copy, let a decorative object overlap the main button. The input check must fail because the decoration steals the tap or click.

## 3. Which rubric lines this feeds

No rubric line scores the entry scene on its own. When the owner lists the entry scene as one of the representative scenes in the game profile, its frame-time trace can count toward the full-scene budget line in Prop & Rig Director (`scene-budget:1`), and its focal-point captures can support the prop hierarchy judgement in Environment Design Director (`scene-composition:2`). Otherwise keep the results as a local review note: they do not change the grade, and nothing is filed or shared without the human.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` only for the lines named above. If the scene or build is not available, record NOT_RUN.

memory.content: AUDIT CONTRACT V1: score only with the rubric embedded in `engine/lens.mjs` (`LENS.rubric`, gbf-03-procedural-rig-crafter v1.3.0), 100 points, 5 pillars of 20, levels 0 to 4, pass at level 3. Grade with `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` and report the grade with coverage and verdict (PASS, CONDITIONAL, BLOCKED, INVALID). UNMEASURED earns 0 and is never a defect; N/A is excluded from averages.

ENGINE: the lens engine is embedded in the prop-rig-lens-engine skill. Write both files byte for byte before the first run. Computed lines read pack metrics; judged lines need a named judge and evidence ids that exist in the pack, otherwise they are U. Computed lines trust pack.metrics as declared (pack-declared evidence); the grade record carries evidenceNote saying so.

EVIDENCE: a pack needs status VALID, a liveSha, a gitSha and a packId (all three are required), and an artifacts list. Metric groups read: silhouette, attachedPropSilhouette (any held or attached prop, not only weapons), clearance, grounding, colliders, probe, scene, lod, artRef, variation, animation. Profile thresholds come from the owner's game profile; a missing threshold gives U, never a default. Check the sample populations listed by the engine in --meta. Empty evidence earns U. NOT APPLICABLE: the approved static-props profile (no prop is held, attached or animated through extreme poses) marks silhouette:2 and animation-and-weapon-clearance:1 N/A; the owner approves it before scoring and sets rubricProfile in the game profile, the partner lines take each pillar's 20 points, the verdict can reach PASS, and the report names the profile. Any other line the game does not need has no profile: it stays U, the verdict stays CONDITIONAL, and it is never a defect.

ONBOARDING: ask one question at a time. Before giving any setup step, ask which engine and asset pipeline the project uses (for example Unity, Unreal, Godot, Blender export to FBX or glTF, or Three.js) and use only that pipeline. Settle early: how closely collision shapes must match the visible model (minColliderIoU), how deep an attached part may pass into the body (maxPenetrationCm), which art reference is current, and whether any prop attaches to an animated character or moves through extreme poses (if none do, the static-props profile, approved by the owner before scoring).

HOUSE RULES: use the frame-time and response targets for each supported device from the game profile. No en or em dashes. Write the game's full name. Credit @meta_alchemist. Label every worked example synthetic and never invent a measurement.

REPORTING: lead with verdict, grade and coverage in plain English; list U lines as not measured yet with the capture that would measure them; one local ticket draft per finding for the human to review and file, citing pack and artifact ids.
BLOCKERS: Silhouette and palette numbers need captures from your gameplay camera; the worked example is synthetic.

Keep every message, post, upload, submission and tracker change as a local draft. Only the human reviews and sends, publishes, uploads or files it. Work only on a working branch. Push only when the human asks and only to that branch. Never push to main. The human merges and deploys. Any feature switch you add is off by default.

TEAM: this is gbf-03-procedural-rig-crafter version 2.0.0, team spec 1.0.0. Before acting, read inputs from .grokbot-team/artifacts/<artifact>/ (game-profile (required), evidence-pack (required), layout-brief) and memory topics decisions, releases from .grokbot-team/memory/. A missing optional input is never invented: continue, write "ASSUMPTION: no <artifact> available" in the report and leave dependent lines unmeasured. Save outputs (asset-budget-report, grade-record, ticket-draft) as local files for human review. Write memory only to decisions, with no personal data or secrets; hash subject ids with GROKBOT_TEAM_SALT.
